title: Subdivision–Ex adjunction on homotopy classes with Kan targets
statement:
Use simplicial sets, Kan complexes and internal functor simplicial sets of [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For simplicial sets $A,B$, put $[A,B]_{\mathrm e}=\pi_0^{\mathrm e}\operatorname{Fun}(A,B)$: maps $A\to B$ modulo the equivalence relation generated by pairs joined by a simplicial homotopy $A\times\Delta^1\to B$. Take $\operatorname{Sd}A$ to be the degreewise colimit over simplices of $A$ of the nerves of posets of nonempty subsets of the corresponding ordinals, and put $(\operatorname{Ex}B)_n=\operatorname{Hom}(N(\mathcal P_+([n])),B)$ with subset-image operators, as in [lem-coef-subdivision-face-poset-calculus]. For every small simplicial set $A$ and every Kan complex $Y$, $\operatorname{Ex}Y$ is Kan, and the natural subdivision–Ex adjunction induces a bijection
$$[\operatorname{Sd}A,Y]_{\mathrm e}\ \cong\ [A,\operatorname{Ex}Y]_{\mathrm e}.$$
More explicitly, two maps $\operatorname{Sd}A\to Y$ represent the same edge-generated homotopy class if and only if their adjoint maps $A\to\operatorname{Ex}Y$ do. The bijection is natural in $A$ and in maps between Kan targets $Y$.

proof.text: First prove the Kan clause directly. A horn inclusion $i:\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ is anodyne by the lifting-property definition: every Kan fibration lifts against it. Also $Y\to\Delta^0$ is a Kan fibration, precisely because $Y$ is Kan. Given $a:\Lambda_k^n\to\operatorname{Ex}Y$, transpose it to $\widetilde a:\operatorname{Sd}\Lambda_k^n\to Y$. Subdivision preservation makes $\operatorname{Sd}(i)$ anodyne, so its lifting property against $Y\to\Delta^0$ extends $\widetilde a$ to $\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to Y$. Transposing back gives a filler for $a$; naturality of the strict adjunction identifies its restriction with $a$. This covers all $n\geq1$ and all $k$, including outer horns, and imposes no dimension-zero nonemptiness condition.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.5.5, expanded by transposing horn lifting against the preservation theorem 00Z3

proof.text: For $e=0,1$, write $i_e:A\to\Delta^1\times A$ for $a\mapsto(e,a)$. Write $f,g:\operatorname{Sd}A\to Y$ and $f^{\prime},g^{\prime}:A\to\operatorname{Ex}Y$ for corresponding maps. For a homotopy $h:\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}A\to Y$, form $h\circ q$, where $q:\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^1\times A)\to\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}A$ has coordinates $\lambda_{\Delta^1}\circ\operatorname{Sd}(\operatorname{pr}_1)$ and $\operatorname{Sd}(\operatorname{pr}_A)$. Transpose $h\circ q$ by the strict adjunction. On the endpoint $e=0,1$, the coordinates of $q\circ\operatorname{Sd}(i_e)$ are the constant vertex $e$ and the identity of $\operatorname{Sd}A$: the first equality follows from naturality of $\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^0=\Delta^0$ (the singleton poset has exactly one nonempty chain, so the face-poset formula gives this identification and its last-vertex map is the identity), and the second from $\operatorname{pr}_A i_e=1_A$. Thus its transpose is a homotopy between $f^{\prime}$ and $g^{\prime}$. Apply this construction to each edge of a zigzag. Only the map induced by the product projections is used; no preservation of products by subdivision is asserted.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.6, explicit prism transpose and converse restriction argument (online reference; archive WANTED)

proof.text: Conversely, start with one homotopy $h^{\prime}:\Delta^1\times A\to\operatorname{Ex}Y$ from $f^{\prime}$ to $g^{\prime}$. Put $T=\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^1\times A)$, $S=\operatorname{Sd}(\{0\}\times A)$, and let $j:S\to T$ be induced by inclusion. Identify $\operatorname{Sd}(\{e\}\times A)$ with $\operatorname{Sd}A$ via the functor applied to the projection isomorphism $\{e\}\times A\cong A$. Transposition gives $u:T\to Y$, with $u\operatorname{Sd}(i_0)=f$ and $u\operatorname{Sd}(i_1)=g$. Put $v=f\circ\operatorname{Sd}(\operatorname{pr}_A)$, so $uj=vj$ and $v\operatorname{Sd}(i_1)=f$. The map $\{0\}\to\Delta^1$ is the horn $\Lambda_0^1\to\Delta^1$, hence anodyne by definition. Apply the pushout-product theorem with the monomorphism $\varnothing\to A$ to get that $\{0\}\times A\to\Delta^1\times A$ is anodyne (interchange the two product coordinates). Subdivision preservation makes $j$ anodyne. Now apply the same theorem to the monomorphism $\partial\Delta^1\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$ and $j$, where $\partial\Delta^1$ is the disjoint union of the two constant-vertex simplicial subsets; its inclusion is injective in each degree. Its domain is $(\Delta^1\times S)\amalg_{\partial\Delta^1\times S}(\partial\Delta^1\times T)$. Define a map from this domain to $Y$ by the constant-in-$\Delta^1$ map $uj=vj$ on $\Delta^1\times S$, and by $u,v$ on the two copies of $T$; equality on the overlap gives a well-defined map. The resulting anodyne map to $\Delta^1\times T$ lifts against $Y\to\Delta^0$, giving $H:\Delta^1\times T\to Y$ with endpoints $u,v$. Restrict along $\Delta^1\times\operatorname{Sd}(i_1)$ to obtain a homotopy from $g$ to $f$. Repeat for each edge of a zigzag of adjoints. No reduction of a zigzag to a single homotopy and no mapping-space fibrancy theorem is needed.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.6, explicit prism transpose and converse restriction argument (online reference; archive WANTED)

proof.text: The strict adjunction is bijective on maps. Step 2 sends every generator of the edge-generated equivalence relation to a generator, and step 3 sends each generator back to an equivalent pair. Applying these observations along finite zigzags gives a well-defined bijection of the stated quotients, with inverse induced by the inverse strict adjunction. For a map $a:A_0\to A_1$, the adjoint of $f\circ\operatorname{Sd}(a)$ is $f^{\prime}\circ a$; for $b:Y\to Y_1$, the adjoint of $b\circ f$ is $\operatorname{Ex}(b)\circ f^{\prime}$. These are the naturality identities of the strict adjunction. Precomposition and postcomposition preserve homotopies by composing the displayed homotopy maps, so the same identities hold on the quotients. This proves naturality for all $a$ and all maps $b$ between Kan targets.

lean.statement: theorem subdivision_ex_homotopy_adjunction : (∀ Y : SSet.{u}, KanComplex Y → KanComplex (ex.obj Y)) ∧ (∀ (A Y : SSet.{u}), KanComplex Y → ∀ (f g : sd.obj A ⟶ Y), π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex f) = π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex g) ↔ π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex ((sdExAdjunction.homEquiv A Y) f)) = π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex ((sdExAdjunction.homEquiv A Y) g))) ∧ ∃ (e : ∀ (A Y : SSet.{u}), KanComplex Y → π₀ ((ihom (sd.obj A)).obj Y) ≃ π₀ ((ihom A).obj (ex.obj Y))), (∀ (A Y : SSet.{u}) (hY : KanComplex Y) (f : sd.obj A ⟶ Y), e A Y hY (π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex f)) = π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex ((sdExAdjunction.homEquiv A Y) f))) ∧ (∀ (A A' Y : SSet.{u}) (hY : KanComplex Y) (a : A' ⟶ A) (f : sd.obj A ⟶ Y), e A' Y hY (π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex (sd.map a ≫ f))) = π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex (a ≫ (sdExAdjunction.homEquiv A Y) f))) ∧ (∀ (A Y Y' : SSet.{u}) (hY : KanComplex Y) (hY' : KanComplex Y') (b : Y ⟶ Y') (f : sd.obj A ⟶ Y), e A Y' hY' (π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex (f ≫ b))) = π₀.mk (Enhanced.diagramVertex ((sdExAdjunction.homEquiv A Y) f ≫ ex.map b)))
